meta.case_name: Profitable Growth Strategy: Student Health Insurance

prompt.context:
Our client is a business unit within a large national health insurance company. The client focuses primarily on the higher-education student health insurance market, selling medical insurance, prescription drug insurance and dental insurance to students at large universities. The client is the market leader, both in terms of customers (~500,000) and revenue (~$500M). The overall market for higher-education student health insurance is estimated at 2.5M potential customers and $2.2B in potential revenue.

This market requires a unique, two-staged sales model. The "first sale" is often made to the on-campus student health center to gain access to the student population. The "second sale" is to the students, who are the ultimate consumers and purchasers of the insurance products. In certain segments of the market, a broker may also act as an intermediary to the school.

The client's operating margins have declined significantly in the face of aggressive competition and shrinking higher education budgets. Additionally, Health Care Reform presents a potential risk for future growth and profitability – notably, students age 26 and under can remain on their parents' health insurance (versus having to buy student health insurance) and health insurers will be required to spend 80% of all revenue on medical expenses. The client's current operating margins are 9%, down from 25% five years ago.

Deloitte Consulting has been engaged to identify profitable avenues of growth for the client as a part of the client's three-year growth strategy. Additionally, we have been asked to deliver prioritized recommendations on potential growth strategies.
prompt.question: What are the potential avenues of growth for the student health insurance company?

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's current market share?
clarifying_info.a: The client has ~500,000 customers and ~$500M revenue. The total market is 2.5M potential customers and $2.2B in potential revenue, implying roughly 20% customer share and 23% revenue share.

clarifying_info.q: What products does the client currently offer?
clarifying_info.a: Medical insurance, prescription drug insurance, and dental insurance to students at large universities.

clarifying_info.q: What is the two-stage sales model?
clarifying_info.a: The first sale is to the on-campus student health center to gain access to the student population. The second sale is to students, who are the ultimate purchasers. A broker may also act as intermediary.

clarifying_info.q: What does Health Care Reform mean for this business?
clarifying_info.a: Students age 26 and under can remain on their parents' health insurance instead of buying student health insurance. Also, health insurers will be required to spend 80% of all premium revenue on medical expenses.

exhibits.title: Student Health Market Size, Revenue Composition, and Select Product Penetration
exhibits.shows: Four charts: (1) distribution of schools by size (number of schools vs. school size in students, with % of all students per band), (2) revenue composition by customer size (small schools <$1M annual revenue vs. large schools >$1M), (3) school and student penetration rates for ancillary products (dental, discount cards, SAP), and (4) product revenue contribution breakdown.
exhibits.data: School size bands: >20K, 10-20K, 5-10K, 1-5K, <1K students. % of all students: 32%, 26%, 20%, 20%, 2%. Note: 90% of the client's 'Large Schools' have >10K students. Revenue composition: small schools vs. large schools (exact split visible in exhibit). School penetration: Dental 52.3%, Discount Cards 7.5%, SAP 6.6%. Student penetration (among medical insurance holders): Dental 42.0%, Discount Cards 19.5%, SAP (minimal). Product revenue contribution: Medical Insurance 99%, Dental ~0.6%, Discount Cards ~0.2%, SAP ~0.2%.

exhibits.title: Data Sheet for Question 3 – Small School Operating Margin Analysis
exhibits.shows: Four product/customer scenarios (A–D) with premium revenue per school, insurance plan pricing, and cost structure components for the small school segment. Also shows client historical financials (revenue and pretax operating income from 2006–2010).
exhibits.data: Scenarios: A=Plus/Large School ($1,000,000 revenue), B=Standard/Large School ($1,000,000 revenue), C=Plus/Small School ($500,000 revenue), D=Standard/Small School ($500,000 revenue). Plus Insurance: $2,000/student/year. Standard Insurance: $1,000/student/year. Costs: Selling Expenses 7% of Premium Revenue; Setup Costs $50,000/school; Administration Costs $50/student; Medical Costs 80% of Premium Revenue. Historical Revenue: $373M (2006), $398M (07), $462M (08), $487M (09), $518M (10). Historical Pretax Operating Income: $88M (2006), $70M (07), $58M (08), $42M (09), $44M (10).

framework: Existing products / existing customers: Defend and grow core business (price optimization, sales force effectiveness, increased penetration of existing products, competitive differentiation, cost leadership)

Existing products / new customers: Identify new segments and channels (pursue small school segment, pursue secondary schools/private/charter schools, pursue individual students where schools do not offer insurance, target uninsured)

New products / existing customers: Develop new products for current customers – schools and students (adjacent insurance products for students such as tuition, electronics, auto, renters; adjacent health services such as mental health and wellness; adjacent services for health centers such as billing)
New products / new customers: Offer new products to new customer segments

questions.prompt: What are the potential avenues of growth for the student health insurance company? (After initial framework, provide Exhibit 1 and ask candidate to synthesize additional recommendations from the data.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should provide a structured framework (e.g., Ansoff matrix or products/markets 2x2) before listing ideas. Key data-driven insights from Exhibit 1: (1) Lower-enrollment schools (<10K students) represent 42% of all students across thousands of schools – an underserved market. (2) Client earns the majority of revenue from large schools (>10K students). (3) Revenue is almost entirely from medical insurance (99%) – very low penetration of dental, discount cards, SAP. (4) There is significant opportunity to increase penetration of ancillary products to existing customers (schools and students).

questions.prompt: Our client felt a large part of the addressable market was not being addressed (the small school market). At a high level, what qualitative and quantitative criteria should the client consider when assessing this market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize this as a market attractiveness assessment and structure criteria across multiple dimensions: (1) Market size – segment market, quantify revenue potential by # schools, # students, insurance requirements, premium projections; (2) Market growth – historic growth rates, projected school counts, healthcare reform trends; (3) Competitive intensity – customer interviews, competitor assessment, market share analysis, win/loss rates; (4) Strategic fit – alignment of required strategy (cost vs. differentiation) with existing business strategy; (5) Capability needs – gap analysis, requisite capital expenditures; (6) Profitability – model margin scenarios under various revenue/cost assumptions; (7) Likely penetration/market capture – sensitivity analysis across growth, competition, margin, and pricing assumptions.

questions.prompt: What type of information would you need to calculate operating margin percentage for the small school segment? Then, using the data sheet, calculate the operating margin percentage for each of the four product/customer scenarios (A, B, C, D).
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for: cost structure (fixed vs. variable), product pricing, number of customers or total revenue. After receiving Exhibit 2, candidate must derive student count per school from price-per-student and total revenue, then apply each cost line. Key observations: fixed costs (setup) are more burdensome for smaller schools; higher-priced Plus product halves admin cost as % of revenue; medical and selling expenses are percentage-based and constant regardless of school size.

math.setup:
For each scenario, derive # students = Premium Revenue / Price Per Student. Then calculate each cost component and sum to get Total Costs. Operating Margin % = (Revenue - Total Costs) / Revenue.

Scenario A (Plus, Large School): Revenue = $1,000,000; Students = $1,000,000 / $2,000 = 500
Scenario B (Standard, Large School): Revenue = $1,000,000; Students = $1,000,000 / $1,000 = 1,000
Scenario C (Plus, Small School): Revenue = $500,000; Students = $500,000 / $2,000 = 250
Scenario D (Standard, Small School): Revenue = $500,000; Students = $500,000 / $1,000 = 500
steps: Scenario A: Medical = 80% x $1M = $800K; Selling = 7% x $1M = $70K; Setup = $50K; Admin = 500 x $50 = $25K; Total = $945K; Margin = ($1M - $945K) / $1M = 5.5%
Scenario B: Medical = 80% x $1M = $800K; Selling = 7% x $1M = $70K; Setup = $50K; Admin = 1,000 x $50 = $50K; Total = $970K; Margin = ($1M - $970K) / $1M = 3.0%
Scenario C: Medical = 80% x $500K = $400K; Selling = 7% x $500K = $35K; Setup = $50K; Admin = 250 x $50 = $12.5K; Total = $497.5K; Margin = ($500K - $497.5K) / $500K = 0.5%
Scenario D: Medical = 80% x $500K = $400K; Selling = 7% x $500K = $35K; Setup = $50K; Admin = 500 x $50 = $25K; Total = $510K; Margin = ($500K - $510K) / $500K = -2.0%
math.answer: Scenario A (Plus/Large): 5.5%; Scenario B (Standard/Large): 3.0%; Scenario C (Plus/Small): 0.5%; Scenario D (Standard/Small): -2.0%. All are well below the current overall operating margin of 9%.

questions.prompt: Given the outcome of your previous operating margin analysis, what recommendations would you develop for the client in terms of pursuing the small school market?
questions.guidance: OK answer: Client should not pursue the segment because it is not profitable enough. Good answer: Client should pursue the market only if it can apply levers to improve profitability – e.g., reduce SG&A or selling costs through process redesign or contract renegotiation. Note: price increases and reducing medical costs are NOT possible under Health Care Reform. Best answer: Client should pursue the market with a fundamentally different business model – create an online B2C model that sells directly to students, bypassing the two intermediaries (brokers and schools), similar to how other industries transitioned to direct online distribution (books, airline tickets).

questions.prompt: Ultimately, multiple opportunities were identified for the client to grow, including increasing share in the core market, pursuing small schools, and selling new products to schools and students. How would you evaluate and prioritize these opportunities?
questions.guidance: Candidate should establish a screening/prioritization framework. Strong components include: (1) Strategic Impact and Fit – competitive differentiation, white space/new market opportunity, disruptive potential, addressing unmet marketplace needs, alignment with current business unit and corporate strategy; (2) Financial Impact – revenue potential (market size), income/margin, administrative cost reduction, future cost avoidance; (3) Cost to Achieve – investment/capital costs, ongoing operating costs; (4) Time to Implement / Ease of Implementation – alignment with existing capabilities, innovation complexity, availability of partners or acquisition targets.

brainstorming.prompt: What new products could the client develop for its current student customers?

categories.name: Adjacent services for health centers (schools)
ideas: Billing services for campus health centers

recommendation: The client should pursue a multi-pronged growth strategy: (1) defend and grow the core large-school market through enhanced sales effectiveness and product penetration, particularly for dental and ancillary products which are significantly underpenetrated; (2) pursue the small school market only with a new, lower-cost business model (e.g., direct online B2C sales to students) that eliminates intermediary costs; (3) develop and cross-sell adjacent products to existing student customers.
risks: Health Care Reform (ACA) limits margin levers: medical cost cannot be reduced below 80% of premium and price increases risk competitive disadvantage
Down-market expansion at current cost structure is unprofitable in all small-school scenarios
Students age 26 and under may remain on parental insurance, reducing addressable student population
Online B2C model requires new capabilities and investment, and may cannibalize the existing two-stage sales model
next_steps: Quantify revenue opportunity from increasing ancillary product (dental, discount cards, SAP) penetration among existing customers
Pilot an online direct-to-student sales model for the small school segment to test unit economics
Conduct competitive analysis to identify win/loss dynamics in the large school segment and opportunities to steal share
Model sensitivity analysis for small school market entry under various cost reduction and pricing scenarios
